signature.caption: A smothered mate at the end of a forcing line

sections.title: How to calculate
paras: Calculation is a method, not a talent. Start by listing candidate moves, and look first at forcing moves: checks, then captures, then threats. Forcing moves limit your opponent’s replies, which keeps the number of lines small enough to work through accurately.

For each candidate, list all of your opponent’s sensible replies, not just the one you expect. A line is only as good as its weakest point, and most calculation mistakes come from a reply that was never considered.
At the end of a line, stop and look at the final position again before you decide it is good. Count material, check for hanging pieces and ask what your opponent will do next.
sections.key: Checks, captures, threats. For every forcing move, list all of the opponent’s replies before going deeper.

sections.title: Visualization basics
paras: Seeing the board in your head starts with knowing it by heart. Strong calculators know the color of every square, which squares share a diagonal, and how many moves a knight needs to get anywhere, without looking.
These exercises have no board on purpose. Answer from your mental picture, then check yourself. Speed comes with repetition.
sections.key: Know the board without seeing it: square colors, diagonals and knight distances.

sections.title: Short forcing lines
paras: These positions need a sequence of a few forcing moves. Find the first move, but don’t play it until you have checked every reasonable reply.
If a reply surprises you on the board, that is useful information: it shows which kind of defensive move you tend to miss.
sections.key: Calculate to the end of the line before you move the first piece.

sections.title: Longer calculations
paras: Longer lines demand discipline. Break them into stages: the forcing start, the position where the opponent has a real choice, and the final position. Re-check each stage before moving on.
Quiet moves in the middle of a forcing line are the hardest to see, for both sides. When a line seems to fizzle out, look for a quiet move that keeps the threat alive.
sections.key: Split long lines into stages and re-check each stage, including quiet moves in the middle.

sections.title: Holding the position in your head
paras: In these exercises the board shows the starting position and stays still. You read a sequence of moves and keep track of the changes in your head, then answer a question about the final position.
Say each move to yourself and picture the piece travelling. Keep track of captures especially: a piece that has left the board is the easiest thing to forget.
The sequences start short and grow longer.
sections.key: Picture each move as you read it, and keep a running count of captures.
